title: Ayyub's call
hookLine: Ayyub calls, harm has touched me and You are the most merciful, and is healed (21:83–84)
carry: harm touched me; you are merciful

lines: TWO PARTS: WHAT HAPPENED, WHO GOD IS.
AYYUB, CALLED JOB IN THE BIBLE.
cards: Some prayers are long, with openings and closings and lists. The one in today's verse has two parts, and neither is a request in so many words.
A man has lost his health and his family, and commentators add his wealth too. They say the trial went on for years; nobody can tell you exactly how many.
When he finally speaks to God about it, he doesn't argue or bargain. He says what happened, and he says who God is. Al-Anbiya keeps it to two verses.
Today, the call of Ayyub, the man the Bible calls Job.

teach.b: Pickthall gives his words this way: "Lo! adversity afflicteth me, and Thou art Most Merciful of all who show mercy." In Arabic it's short enough to hold in one breath. Massaniya ad-durr: harm has touched me.
The verb massa means to touch. He doesn't say harm crushed me. He says it touched me, which some commentators read as courtesy, a man choosing his words carefully even in pain.
Then: wa anta arhamu r-rahimin, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Notice what's missing. There is no heal me.
He lays the wound next to the mercy and leaves the rest to God. The next verse says God answered.
The harm was removed, and his family given back to him, with the like of them besides, as a mercy and a reminder.
Surah Sad adds a little: he is told to strike the ground with his foot, and there is cool water to wash in and drink.

teach.h: PATIENT, AND HONEST ABOUT THE PAIN.
teach.b: And God calls him patient, an excellent servant. That's the surprise. The Qur'an praises Ayyub's patience in the same story where he tells God plainly that he's hurting.
So patience here isn't silence. Ya'qub says something close in Surah Yusuf: he takes his grief to God and to no one else.
Some scholars draw a line: complaining about God to people is one thing; telling God is part of the prayer. You may have heard longer tales of Ayyub, with details of his illness and his wife.
Those are stories people tell, from later collections. The Qur'an itself stays brief.

how: Many Muslims recite Ayyub's words from 21:83 in times of illness or hardship, often in Arabic, as a short personal supplication alongside the daily prayers.

o: a complaint about God made to his friends
a two-part prayer: naming the harm and God's mercy
a long plea asking God to heal and restore him

games.q: inside Ayyub's call — tap the pairs.

s: Ayyub's words in 21:83 say 'heal me' outright
they name the harm and name God's mercy. the healing comes in the next verse, as the answer.
Surah Sad calls him patient and an excellent servant, in the same story where he tells God he's hurting.
the long tales of Ayyub's illness come from the Qur'an
the Qur'an keeps his story brief. the longer details are stories people tell, from later collections.

games.q: you've lost your health, your wealth and your family. you finally speak to God about it. what do you say?
o: list everything that went wrong, and ask why.
say harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful.
say nothing at all, to prove you're patient.
games.why: two short parts, and no direct request. God answers anyway, and still calls him patient.

practice: Find one thing that hurts right now, a worry, a loss, a body that aches, and give it a few plain words, the way Ayyub did, without explaining or arguing.
If you pray, you can say his line, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful, and stop there. If you don't, name the hurt to yourself, kindly, and let it sit beside you.

wordCard.voice: Ayyub's call. Two parts: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful. Named, not argued. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: harm has touched me. Ayyub's words in 21:83.

carryVoice: Your line: harm touched me; you are merciful. Patience can still say where it hurts. That's day four hundred eighty-two.
